_source: Old & New pack, content version 1 (Sept 2026). Regenerate if the questions are revised.

questions.q: Who was instructed to build an ark before the flood?
c: Moses
Abraham
Jacob
Noah
questions.a: Noah
questions.x: God gives Noah the dimensions and instructions for the ark.

questions.q: What did Abraham name the son born to Sarah?
c: Isaac
Ishmael
Esau
Joseph
questions.a: Isaac
questions.x: The passage names Sarah's son Isaac.

questions.q: Who approaches the bush that burns without being consumed?
c: Moses
Aaron
Joshua
Caleb
questions.a: Moses
questions.x: Moses is tending a flock when he sees the bush.

questions.q: Which city's walls fall after Israel's procession and shout?
c: Jericho
Ai
Bethel
Shiloh
questions.a: Jericho
questions.x: Joshua 6 describes the fall of Jericho.

questions.q: Which boy repeatedly runs to Eli after hearing his name called?
c: Samuel
David
Jonathan
Solomon
questions.a: Samuel
questions.x: Samuel initially thinks Eli is calling him.

questions.q: Who strikes down Goliath with a sling and a stone?
c: Saul
Jonathan
Abner
David
questions.a: David
questions.x: David confronts Goliath and strikes him with the stone.

questions.q: What does Solomon ask for when God invites him to make a request?
c: A longer life than other kings
The death of his enemies
Riches beyond every neighboring kingdom
An understanding heart to judge the people
questions.a: An understanding heart to judge the people
questions.x: Solomon requests discernment for governing the people.

questions.q: Who is delivered alive from the lions' den in this passage?
c: Abednego
Daniel
Shadrach
Meshach
questions.a: Daniel
questions.x: The king finds Daniel alive after the night in the den.

questions.q: Which queen asks the king to spare her life and the lives of her people?
c: Jezebel
Athaliah
Esther
Vashti
questions.a: Esther
questions.x: Esther identifies the threat against herself and her people at the banquet.

questions.q: Who commits to remain with Naomi and go where she goes?
c: Ruth
Orpah
Rachel
Leah
questions.a: Ruth
questions.x: Ruth refuses to leave Naomi and pledges to accompany her.

questions.q: Who leads the women with tambourines after the sea crossing?
c: Huldah
Miriam
Deborah
Hannah
questions.a: Miriam
questions.x: Miriam takes a tambourine and leads the women in the response.

questions.q: To which city does Jonah deliver his warning in this chapter?
c: Babylon
Samaria
Nineveh
Jerusalem
questions.a: Nineveh
questions.x: Jonah goes to Nineveh with the message he is given.

questions.q: Who picks up Elijah's fallen mantle after Elijah is taken away?
c: Elisha
Isaiah
Jeremiah
Ezekiel
questions.a: Elisha
questions.x: Elisha takes up the mantle and returns to the Jordan.

questions.q: Which woman is described as a prophetess who judged Israel?
c: Ruth
Esther
Abigail
Deborah
questions.a: Deborah
questions.x: Israelites come to Deborah for judgment.

questions.q: What rebuilding work does Nehemiah urge the people to undertake here?
c: The wall of Jerusalem
The walls of Jericho
The palace of Pharaoh
The tower of Babel
questions.a: The wall of Jerusalem
questions.x: Nehemiah calls the people to rebuild Jerusalem's wall.

questions.q: In which town is Jesus born during Joseph and Mary's journey?
c: Bethlehem
Nazareth
Capernaum
Bethany
questions.a: Bethlehem
questions.x: Joseph goes to Bethlehem, and Mary gives birth while they are there.

questions.q: Who baptizes Jesus in the Jordan?
c: Peter
James
Andrew
John
questions.a: John
questions.x: Mark identifies John as the one baptizing Jesus.

questions.q: At the wedding in Cana, what change do the servants discover?
c: Oil has become water
Wine has become salt
Water has become wine
Stones have become bread
questions.a: Water has become wine
questions.x: The water drawn from the jars is tasted as wine.

questions.q: What work are Simon and Andrew doing when Jesus calls them by the sea?
c: Collecting taxes
Repairing a city gate
Tending a vineyard
Casting a fishing net
questions.a: Casting a fishing net
questions.x: They are casting a net because they are fishermen.

questions.q: Which pair are named as Lazarus' sisters?
c: Martha and Mary
Mary and Elizabeth
Priscilla and Phoebe
Joanna and Susanna
questions.a: Martha and Mary
questions.x: John identifies Lazarus with his sisters Mary and Martha.

questions.q: Who climbs a tree to see Jesus passing through Jericho?
c: Nicodemus
Bartimaeus
Jairus
Zacchaeus
questions.a: Zacchaeus
questions.x: Zacchaeus climbs because the crowd prevents him from seeing.

questions.q: Which disciple denies knowing Jesus three times in this scene?
c: Philip
Andrew
Peter
Thomas
questions.a: Peter
questions.x: Peter's three denials are followed by the rooster crowing.

questions.q: What message do the women receive about Jesus at the tomb?
c: He has remained asleep in the tomb
He has risen and is not there
He has moved his teaching to the temple
He has been crowned king in Jerusalem
questions.a: He has risen and is not there
questions.x: The messenger announces that Jesus has risen and points to where he had been laid.

questions.q: Which event is being celebrated when the disciples are filled with the Holy Spirit in this passage?
c: Passover
Purim
The Feast of Dedication
Pentecost
questions.a: Pentecost
questions.x: The chapter opens by naming the day of Pentecost.

questions.q: Toward which city is Saul traveling when he encounters the light and hears Jesus' voice?
c: Damascus
Antioch
Ephesus
Rome
questions.a: Damascus
questions.x: Saul is approaching Damascus on the journey described.

questions.q: What trade is associated with Lydia when Paul meets her?
c: Collecting Roman taxes
Selling purple goods
Making tents
Fishing on the lake
questions.a: Selling purple goods
questions.x: Acts describes Lydia as a seller of purple.

questions.q: What are Paul and Silas doing at midnight in prison?
c: Building a shelter
Praying and singing hymns
Negotiating with the magistrates
Planning a market journey
questions.a: Praying and singing hymns
questions.x: Other prisoners are listening as Paul and Silas pray and sing.

questions.q: Who identifies himself at the beginning of the letter to the Romans?
c: James
Jude
Paul
Peter
questions.a: Paul
questions.x: The opening names Paul and addresses those in Rome.

questions.q: Which quality appears in Paul's list of the fruit of the Spirit?
c: Jealousy
Anger
Patience
Rivalry
questions.a: Patience
questions.x: Patience is included among the fruit listed.

questions.q: In Paul's armor imagery, what is associated with the shield?
c: Truth
Faith
Righteousness
Salvation
questions.a: Faith
questions.x: Paul speaks of the shield of faith.

questions.q: After Jacob dies, Joseph's brothers fear revenge. Which response best explains Joseph's decision to provide for them?
c: He distinguishes their harmful intention from the preservation of many lives.
He concludes that their actions had never been wrong.
He transfers responsibility for their actions to their father.
He demands that they earn food by repaying his imprisonment.
questions.a: He distinguishes their harmful intention from the preservation of many lives.
questions.x: Joseph names the intended harm but also the resulting preservation of life, and promises provision.

questions.q: Some Israelites keep ordinary-day manna overnight and others search for it on the Sabbath. What common problem do these actions reveal?
c: They demonstrate that the sixth day's double portion was unnecessary.
They disregard the different instructions for daily gathering and Sabbath rest.
They follow the same gathering instruction correctly on every day.
They preserve a reserve that Moses had ordered for the whole week.
questions.a: They disregard the different instructions for daily gathering and Sabbath rest.
questions.x: The daily limit and sixth-day exception both require following the instructions actually given.

questions.q: Why does Jethro recommend appointing capable judges rather than having Moses decide every dispute?
c: Moses must stop teaching the people God's instructions.
Every dispute should be left for the people to resolve without judges.
The judges should replace Moses in bringing difficult matters to God.
Shared responsibility can relieve both Moses and the waiting people.
questions.a: Shared responsibility can relieve both Moses and the waiting people.
questions.x: Jethro retains Moses' teaching and difficult-case responsibilities while distributing ordinary cases.

questions.q: Rahab receives a promise of protection. What must her household do for the agreed protection to apply?
c: Wait outside the city wall beside the cord.
Gather in her house, where the scarlet cord identifies it.
Scatter among neighboring houses to avoid being noticed.
Leave Jericho individually before the spies return.
questions.a: Gather in her house, where the scarlet cord identifies it.
questions.x: The spies specify the marked house and warn against going outside it.

questions.q: Boaz tells Ruth to stay with his workers and orders extra grain left for her. What does this combination accomplish?
c: It releases the workers from harvesting the field.
It requires Ruth to repay Naomi before receiving grain.
It prevents Ruth from returning home with what she gathers.
It joins personal protection with practical access to food.
questions.a: It joins personal protection with practical access to food.
questions.x: Boaz provides safety among his workers and directs them to leave grain for her.

questions.q: Why does Hannah bring Samuel to Eli after he is weaned?
c: She is demanding that Eli compensate her for raising him.
She is fulfilling her commitment to dedicate the child she prayed for.
She is asking Eli to choose a different name for him.
She is returning him because her prayer was unanswered.
questions.a: She is fulfilling her commitment to dedicate the child she prayed for.
questions.x: Hannah connects the answered prayer with giving Samuel to the LORD.

questions.q: Saul defends keeping livestock by saying it was intended for sacrifice. How does Samuel answer that defense?
c: The people rather than the king were the only ones accountable.
Obedience cannot be replaced by offering what was taken through disobedience.
A sufficiently large sacrifice makes any command optional.
The command concerned only Saul's private intentions.
questions.a: Obedience cannot be replaced by offering what was taken through disobedience.
questions.x: Samuel contrasts obedience with sacrifice in response to Saul's explanation.

questions.q: Why is Nathan's account of the rich man taking the poor man's lamb effective in confronting David?
c: David condemns an injustice before Nathan exposes his own related wrongdoing.
David first agrees that a king is exempt from ordinary moral duties.
The story proves that David had stolen an actual sheep.
The story allows Nathan to avoid mentioning David's conduct.
questions.a: David condemns an injustice before Nathan exposes his own related wrongdoing.
questions.x: David's judgment of the story prepares the direct accusation against him.

questions.q: Naaman initially rejects Elisha's instruction to wash in the Jordan. What do his servants help him reconsider?
c: The instruction changes from seven washings to one.
A simple instruction is still worth obeying when he would have attempted a difficult one.
The Jordan is described as medically superior to every other river.
Elisha requires him to pay before washing.
questions.a: A simple instruction is still worth obeying when he would have attempted a difficult one.
questions.x: The servants contrast willingness to attempt a great task with rejection of a simple direction.

questions.q: Elisha is angry when Joash strikes the ground only three times. How does the passage connect the action to its announced result?
c: The limited strikes correspond to limited victories rather than complete defeat of Syria.
The strikes determine the number of years Elisha will remain alive.
The arrows represent three battles Israel has already lost.
Joash's action cancels the earlier promise of any victory.
questions.a: The limited strikes correspond to limited victories rather than complete defeat of Syria.
questions.x: Elisha says additional strikes would have meant a more complete victory.

questions.q: Esther explains the danger of approaching the king uninvited, then asks for a fast. What changes in her response?
c: She learns that the law has already been repealed.
She receives a guarantee that she cannot die.
She asks Mordecai to make the appeal while she leaves the palace.
She decides to act despite the danger rather than treat the danger as a reason to remain silent.
questions.a: She decides to act despite the danger rather than treat the danger as a reason to remain silent.
questions.x: Her final response accepts the risk and commits to approaching the king.

questions.q: How does the plant episode answer Jonah's anger about Nineveh?
c: It contrasts Jonah's concern for a plant with God's concern for a large city.
It proves the city had earned mercy by planting trees.
It tells Jonah that compassion applies only to Israelites.
It explains why the plant's survival is more important than human life.
questions.a: It contrasts Jonah's concern for a plant with God's concern for a large city.
questions.x: The final question moves from Jonah's pity for the plant to concern for Nineveh.

questions.q: When threats against Jerusalem increase, how do the builders respond?
c: They finish the wall before taking the threat seriously.
They combine prayer with guards and an adjusted work arrangement.
They abandon prayer because defensive action replaces it.
They abandon the wall because prayer makes construction unnecessary.
questions.a: They combine prayer with guards and an adjusted work arrangement.
questions.x: The narrative combines prayer, watchfulness, and continued work.

questions.q: What distinguishes the Bereans' reception of Paul's message?
c: They accept it only because Paul is a visiting teacher.
They reject it without listening because it is unfamiliar.
They test it by counting how many people have already believed.
They welcome the message and examine the Scriptures to assess it.
questions.a: They welcome the message and examine the Scriptures to assess it.
questions.x: Their readiness to receive is joined to daily examination of the Scriptures.

questions.q: A complaint arises that some widows are neglected in the daily distribution. What does the proposed response preserve?
c: Teaching alone, by ending the food distribution.
Distribution alone, by ending the ministry of the word.
Unity by refusing to investigate complaints from one language group.
Care for the neglected group alongside the apostles' prayer and teaching work.
questions.a: Care for the neglected group alongside the apostles' prayer and teaching work.
questions.x: The community appoints people to the practical responsibility while the apostles retain theirs.

questions.q: The prison doors open, yet Paul calls out to the jailer. Why is that intervention decisive in the scene?
c: Paul asks the jailer to punish the other prisoners first.
Paul prevents the jailer from harming himself by telling him the prisoners are still there.
Paul tells him that all the prisoners have escaped safely.
Paul demands release before responding to the immediate danger.
questions.a: Paul prevents the jailer from harming himself by telling him the prisoners are still there.
questions.x: The jailer assumes an escape and is about to kill himself; Paul's words interrupt that action.

questions.q: Why does Paul frame his request about Onesimus as an appeal rather than simply issuing an order?
c: He seeks willing action grounded in love, with Onesimus received as a beloved brother.
He says that Onesimus has become unrelated to the Christian community.
He wants to prevent Philemon from having any choice in the matter.
He presents Onesimus as valuable only while imprisoned.
questions.a: He seeks willing action grounded in love, with Onesimus received as a beloved brother.
questions.x: Paul explicitly contrasts compulsion with voluntary goodness and calls Onesimus a brother.

questions.q: Some believers eat well while others remain hungry at the common meal. Which practical instruction directly addresses this division?
c: Replace the common gathering with a contest over portions.
Wait for one another, and satisfy ordinary hunger at home.
Reserve the gathering for those who can afford to bring more food.
Eat quickly so others will not notice the difference.
questions.a: Wait for one another, and satisfy ordinary hunger at home.
questions.x: Paul connects their humiliating divisions with instructions to wait and eat at home when hungry.

questions.q: In Jesus' explanation of the sower, how does the thorny soil differ from the rocky soil?
c: Competing cares and desires choke the word, rather than trouble exposing a lack of root.
It never receives the word in any form.
It loses the word immediately to birds on the path.
It produces a smaller but explicitly fruitful harvest.
questions.a: Competing cares and desires choke the word, rather than trouble exposing a lack of root.
questions.x: The thorny hearers face choking cares, riches, and desires; the rocky hearers fall away under pressure.

questions.q: Martha asks Jesus to make Mary help her. What does his response emphasize?
c: Mary must leave because women may not listen to teaching.
Martha's anxious distraction should not displace the good portion Mary has chosen.
Hospitality is forbidden for all disciples.
Listening is acceptable only after every possible task is complete.
questions.a: Martha's anxious distraction should not displace the good portion Mary has chosen.
questions.x: Jesus addresses Martha's worry and defends Mary's choice to listen.

questions.q: How does Zacchaeus' stated response differ from the crowd's complaint about Jesus visiting him?
c: He refuses to welcome Jesus while they offer their own homes.
He commits to generosity and restitution while they focus on his reputation as a sinner.
He demands gifts from the crowd while they ask him to repay victims.
He denies ever possessing wealth while they ask him to give it away.
questions.a: He commits to generosity and restitution while they focus on his reputation as a sinner.
questions.x: The crowd objects to the visitor's association; Zacchaeus announces concrete changes concerning possessions and fraud.

questions.q: Jesus washes the disciples' feet and then explains his action. What makes the example challenging to ordinary assumptions about rank?
c: He makes service the duty of only the lowest-ranked disciple.
He requires them to hire others to repeat the act.
The one acknowledged as Teacher and Lord performs a service they should extend to one another.
Jesus denies being their teacher so that service will no longer seem surprising.
questions.a: The one acknowledged as Teacher and Lord performs a service they should extend to one another.
questions.x: Jesus affirms his position while making his service an example for them.

questions.q: As the healed man is repeatedly questioned, what becomes clearer about the dispute?
c: The questioning ends because nobody disputes the healing or its implications.
His testimony about receiving sight clashes with the interrogators' conclusions about Jesus.
Everyone agrees on Jesus' identity before the questioning begins.
His parents volunteer a full explanation of how the healing happened.
questions.a: His testimony about receiving sight clashes with the interrogators' conclusions about Jesus.
questions.x: The man maintains the reality of his sight while the authorities contest what it means about Jesus.

questions.q: What is the sequence of the travelers' encounter on the way to Emmaus?
c: They return to Jerusalem before he joins them on the road.
They recognize him only after a new burial is arranged.
Jesus interprets Scripture on the road; they recognize him at the meal and return to Jerusalem.
They recognize him immediately, then ask him to explain why the tomb is occupied.
questions.a: Jesus interprets Scripture on the road; they recognize him at the meal and return to Jerusalem.
questions.x: The narrative moves from interpretation during the walk to recognition at the table and return.

questions.q: Why does Jesus ask whether forgiveness or commanding the man to walk is easier to say?
c: He asks the teachers to perform the healing instead.
He withdraws his earlier statement of forgiveness.
He connects the visible healing with his claim to authority to forgive sins.
He agrees that the man's condition cannot change.
questions.a: He connects the visible healing with his claim to authority to forgive sins.
questions.x: Jesus announces the healing so those present may know the Son of Man's authority to forgive.

questions.q: After the storm is calmed, why do the disciples ask who Jesus is?
c: They think another boat secretly calmed the storm.
They are deciding which disciple should receive credit.
The obedience of wind and sea confronts them with the extent of his authority.
They have forgotten the name of the person in their boat.
questions.a: The obedience of wind and sea confronts them with the extent of his authority.
questions.x: Their question follows their fear and amazement at the wind and sea obeying him.

questions.q: What contrast drives the judgment against the unforgiving servant?
c: He is punished because he has never owed the king anything.
He receives extraordinary mercy but refuses mercy to a fellow servant.
He pays the king fully but cannot collect a lawful salary.
He forgives his fellow servant before the king refuses him mercy.
questions.a: He receives extraordinary mercy but refuses mercy to a fellow servant.
questions.x: The king's cancellation of his debt exposes the inconsistency of his subsequent refusal.

questions.q: Why does the landowner reject the first workers' complaint about equal payment?
c: He admits he paid the first workers less than agreed.
He claims the last workers secretly worked the longest.
He announces that nobody will receive the promised wage.
He has honored their agreement, while choosing generosity toward those hired later.
questions.a: He has honored their agreement, while choosing generosity toward those hired later.
questions.x: The response distinguishes the agreed wage from resentment at generosity to others.

questions.q: Why does the rich man's plan fail within the parable?
c: He gives away the entire crop and is then criticized for generosity.
He plans secure enjoyment from stored goods without accounting for the imminent loss of his life.
His land produces nothing after years of work.
His barns are destroyed by neighbors before harvest.
questions.a: He plans secure enjoyment from stored goods without accounting for the imminent loss of his life.
questions.x: The surprise is that the life for which he plans is required that night.

questions.q: Paul imagines a foot feeling excluded and an eye dismissing a hand. What problem do these two examples address together?
c: The body's healthiest members are those needing no other member.
Difference of function is a defect the body must eliminate.
Both self-exclusion and contempt for others misunderstand the body's mutual dependence.
Only members with the same function can belong to one body.
questions.a: Both self-exclusion and contempt for others misunderstand the body's mutual dependence.
questions.x: The two directions of comparison expose both inferiority and superiority as mistaken responses to different roles.

questions.q: Compare the reasons given for Sabbath observance in these two passages. Which account preserves both the shared command and the different rationale?
c: Both command rest; Exodus recalls creation, while Deuteronomy recalls deliverance from slavery.
Both command rest; Exodus recalls slavery, while Deuteronomy recalls the creation of the world.
Exodus commands rest for household heads; Deuteronomy first extends it to servants and livestock.
Exodus ties rest to harvest success; Deuteronomy replaces that reason with a wilderness journey.
questions.a: Both command rest; Exodus recalls creation, while Deuteronomy recalls deliverance from slavery.
questions.x: Exodus appeals to creation and includes servants and animals; Deuteronomy emphasizes remembered slavery and deliverance.

questions.q: Paul asks whether Abraham's faith was counted as righteousness before or after circumcision. What work does that chronology do in his argument?
c: It lets him identify circumcision as the event that first caused Abraham to believe God's promise.
It lets him restrict Abraham's fatherhood to descendants who received the sign before they believed.
It lets him treat Genesis' account of faith as a later explanation of an earlier circumcision.
It lets him describe Abraham as father of believing uncircumcised people as well as circumcised people who share his faith.
questions.a: It lets him describe Abraham as father of believing uncircumcised people as well as circumcised people who share his faith.
questions.x: Paul uses the before-circumcision timing to support fatherhood across the circumcision boundary, with faith central.

questions.q: Hebrews develops an argument from Melchizedek blessing Abraham and receiving a tenth. Which claim goes beyond the evidence used in that argument?
c: Genesis explicitly identifies Melchizedek as a biological descendant of Levi.
The one receiving the blessing is treated as lesser than the one bestowing it.
Abraham's payment of a tenth contributes to the argument about Melchizedek's greatness.
Levi's relation to Abraham is used to connect the comparison to later priestly tithes.
questions.a: Genesis explicitly identifies Melchizedek as a biological descendant of Levi.
questions.x: The argument invokes Abraham's ancestor relationship to Levi; Genesis does not supply a Levitical descent for Melchizedek.

questions.q: John compares the Son of Man being lifted up with Moses' serpent. Which reading retains the stated point without turning every detail into an identity claim?
c: The comparison establishes that the bronze object itself is the source of the world's salvation.
The comparison requires the Son of Man to have caused the wilderness bites before he can save.
The comparison limits the promised life to Israelites who were physically present with Moses.
The comparison connects being lifted up with life received, while John names belief as the response.
questions.a: The comparison connects being lifted up with life received, while John names belief as the response.
questions.x: John connects lifting up and life, then speaks of everyone who believes; it does not identify every narrative detail.

questions.q: John reports that Jesus' legs were not broken after the soldiers found him already dead. What combination best explains how John presents that detail?
c: John treats the no-broken-bone instruction as a command addressed directly to Roman soldiers.
A concrete execution detail is interpreted through Scripture's requirement that no bone be broken.
The soldiers deliberately follow Moses' Passover instructions as their announced reason for stopping.
The absence of broken legs is presented as evidence that Jesus had not actually died.
questions.a: A concrete execution detail is interpreted through Scripture's requirement that no bone be broken.
questions.x: John narrates the soldiers' finding and then supplies a scriptural interpretation; he does not attribute that interpretation to them.

questions.q: Why is Jesus' answer about bread more than a refusal to perform a food miracle when read with the cited Deuteronomy context?
c: Both scenes require proving sonship by manufacturing bread before trusting God's speech.
Both scenes describe people who had never received any provision in a wilderness.
Both scenes connect hunger and testing with dependence on what God says.
Both scenes argue that material food is inherently incompatible with obedience.
questions.a: Both scenes connect hunger and testing with dependence on what God says.
questions.x: Deuteronomy interprets hunger and manna as instruction in dependence, which gives depth to Jesus' wilderness reply.

questions.q: Which comparison best connects Ezekiel's failed shepherds with Jesus' description of the good shepherd?
c: Self-serving neglect and abandonment are contrasted with care that seeks the sheep and accepts personal cost.
Both texts commend shepherds who protect themselves by leaving threatened sheep behind.
Both texts define successful care primarily as extracting greater material benefit from the flock.
Ezekiel praises the rulers' care, while John introduces the first criticism of negligent shepherds.
questions.a: Self-serving neglect and abandonment are contrasted with care that seeks the sheep and accepts personal cost.
questions.x: Ezekiel condemns leaders who feed themselves and neglect sheep; John contrasts the good shepherd's self-giving with a hireling's flight.

questions.q: How does the contrast among sailors, Ninevites, and Jonah complicate a simple insider-versus-outsider reading?
c: Jonah's anger is directed at the Ninevites for refusing to repent after his warning.
The outsiders respond with reverence or repentance, while the prophet resents the mercy shown to Nineveh.
The outsiders consistently refuse to respond, while Jonah alone welcomes the city's deliverance.
The sailors and Ninevites receive approval because the narrative portrays them as Israelites.
questions.a: The outsiders respond with reverence or repentance, while the prophet resents the mercy shown to Nineveh.
questions.x: The sailors fear the LORD, Nineveh turns from evil, and Jonah is displeased by God's relenting.

questions.q: The nearer relative first agrees to redeem the field, then declines when Ruth is included. What is the strongest explanation of that change supported by the scene?
c: The fuller transaction raises a concern about his own inheritance that the land offer alone had not resolved.
He learns that Boaz has already purchased the land, making any further decision legally unnecessary.
He discovers that Ruth has no connection to the deceased family, removing the reason for redemption.
He changes his mind because the elders refuse to witness any arrangement involving Boaz.
questions.a: The fuller transaction raises a concern about his own inheritance that the land offer alone had not resolved.
questions.x: The relative explicitly cites harm to his own inheritance after the implications concerning Ruth and the deceased man's name are stated.

questions.q: A reader says Israel's king may accumulate wealth and treat fellow Israelites as inherently inferior. Which comparison best tests that claim?
c: Deuteronomy restricts royal accumulation and pride; Samuel warns how a king will take from the people.
Deuteronomy commands royal accumulation; Samuel restricts only the people's ability to complain.
Both passages define unrestricted accumulation as the evidence of a king's faithfulness.
Samuel removes every restriction in Deuteronomy by announcing the duties of kingship.
questions.a: Deuteronomy restricts royal accumulation and pride; Samuel warns how a king will take from the people.
questions.x: The royal instructions limit wealth and a lifted-up heart; Samuel's repeated taking functions as warning.

questions.q: How does Hebrews handle the tension between Psalm 8's language of subjection and what its audience presently sees?
c: It claims the audience already sees every part of the promised subjection without exception.
It concludes that the psalm cannot be used because present observation does not fully match it.
It acknowledges that all things are not yet seen subject, then directs attention to Jesus crowned after suffering death.
It denies that Psalm 8 ever speaks of anything being placed under human feet.
questions.a: It acknowledges that all things are not yet seen subject, then directs attention to Jesus crowned after suffering death.
questions.x: Hebrews states the not-yet-seen condition and contrasts it with seeing Jesus crowned with glory and honor.

questions.q: Jesus cites the desire for mercy rather than sacrifice while answering criticism of his table company. What connection is strongest?
c: Hosea's statement establishes that religious people must avoid eating with anyone called a sinner.
Jesus uses the quotation to deny that the people at the meal have any need for repentance or healing.
The quotation proves that Hosea was originally describing this particular meal with Matthew.
A prophetic criticism of deficient covenant loyalty helps challenge a response that overlooks mercy toward those needing help.
questions.a: A prophetic criticism of deficient covenant loyalty helps challenge a response that overlooks mercy toward those needing help.
questions.x: Hosea criticizes fleeting loyalty; Jesus applies the mercy emphasis through the physician-and-sick comparison.

questions.q: Which conclusion best fits the relationship between worship and conduct in both prophetic rebukes?
c: The problem is that the people have offered too few assemblies and sacrifices.
The criticism is confined to incorrect musical instruments and says nothing about social conduct.
Both prophets say that justice can be postponed until ritual activity has become more elaborate.
Ritual activity does not offset injustice; the rebukes demand a changed treatment of others.
questions.a: Ritual activity does not offset injustice; the rebukes demand a changed treatment of others.
questions.x: Both passages reject worship disconnected from justice; Isaiah specifically names the oppressed, fatherless, and widow.

questions.q: How should the promise of a future return be related to the instructions to build houses and seek the city's welfare?
c: The promise cancels the instructions because any meaningful residence in the city would show unbelief.
The instructions mean that return is ruled out and no future change is promised.
The promise guarantees that each individual exile will return before any family is established there.
The promised future is paired with faithful long-term life in exile, not an instruction to suspend ordinary responsibilities.
questions.a: The promised future is paired with faithful long-term life in exile, not an instruction to suspend ordinary responsibilities.
questions.x: The letter combines settling, praying for the city, and a stated future horizon of seventy years.

questions.q: The people weep when they hear the law, but are instructed to celebrate and share portions. What prevents treating the celebration as indifference to the reading?
c: The shared meal is restricted to those who can already provide their own portions.
Their joy is explicitly linked to understanding the words, and the celebration includes provision for those without prepared food.
The leaders state that the reading was mistaken and should therefore be forgotten.
The people celebrate because understanding is declared unnecessary for obedience.
questions.a: Their joy is explicitly linked to understanding the words, and the celebration includes provision for those without prepared food.
questions.x: The chapter links understanding with both the emotional response and the subsequent joyful, shared observance.

questions.q: What limitation does the opening scene and the final rebuke place on the friends' explanations of Job's suffering?
c: The final rebuke declares that Job's friends have spoken rightly and Job must adopt their explanations.
Readers should not treat their accusations as authoritative merely because those speeches occur in Scripture.
Their accusations must be correct because every character's explanation has the narrator's endorsement.
The opening scene presents Job's suffering as punishment for the specific crimes later alleged by his friends.
questions.a: Readers should not treat their accusations as authoritative merely because those speeches occur in Scripture.
questions.x: The opening affirms Job's integrity, and the ending explicitly rebukes the friends' speech about God.

questions.q: Two adjacent proverbs say not to answer a fool according to folly and to answer a fool according to folly. Which reading best accounts for the different stated consequences?
c: The pair demands judgment about whether a reply would make one resemble the fool or leave the fool self-confident.
The second sentence erases the first, leaving only a universal command to respond.
The first sentence erases the second, leaving only a universal command to remain silent.
Both sentences have identical purposes and make no distinction between the risks of responding and not responding.
questions.a: The pair demands judgment about whether a reply would make one resemble the fool or leave the fool self-confident.
questions.x: One warns against becoming like the fool; the other against leaving the fool wise in his own eyes.

questions.q: What common fault appears in James' seating example and Paul's account of the meal, despite their different settings?
c: Both communities are criticized for giving poorer members exactly the same treatment as richer members.
Both passages require wealth differences to determine who may hear teaching or receive food.
The criticism concerns only private attitudes because no public behavior is described.
Differences in wealth become grounds for humiliation or preferential treatment within the gathered community.
questions.a: Differences in wealth become grounds for humiliation or preferential treatment within the gathered community.
questions.x: James describes favorable seating for the rich; Paul describes hungry members being humiliated at the meal.

questions.q: A believer offers good wishes to someone lacking necessities but withholds practical help. How do both passages assess the gap?
c: The gap matters only when the needy person belongs to a different community.
Words claiming care are inadequate when the speaker can help but refuses action.
Good wishes become sufficient if the speaker repeats them with stronger feeling.
Material assistance is treated as a distraction from the more important act of speaking.
questions.a: Words claiming care are inadequate when the speaker can help but refuses action.
questions.x: Both examples expose a contradiction between expressed faith or love and withheld practical care.

questions.q: How do these passages qualify an appeal to personal freedom about food?
c: Both passages make eating the disputed food mandatory as a demonstration of mature faith.
The effects of one's action on another's conscience can require restraint even when the food itself is not the decisive issue.
Anyone with greater knowledge is instructed to ignore a weaker conscience as irrelevant.
The only permitted response is to declare every kind of food inherently unclean for every person.
questions.a: The effects of one's action on another's conscience can require restraint even when the food itself is not the decisive issue.
questions.x: Both arguments move from knowledge or conviction to responsibility for a vulnerable fellow believer.

questions.q: How does the account of Christ's humiliation function within the preceding instructions about others?
c: It tells believers to secure higher rank before considering anyone else's interests.
It limits concern for others to cases where doing so increases one's present social status.
It supplies the pattern of self-giving humility that the community is told to adopt in its relationships.
It interrupts the ethical instructions with an example explicitly said to be irrelevant to ordinary believers.
questions.a: It supplies the pattern of self-giving humility that the community is told to adopt in its relationships.
questions.x: The passage introduces Christ's example through a call to share his mindset after instructions about humility and others' interests.

questions.q: Why does the discussion of wilderness unbelief lead into a continuing call to enter rest?
c: The argument says hearing the promise alone guarantees entrance regardless of faith or disobedience.
The earlier failure serves as a warning while the later appeal to Today shows the promise still addresses hearers.
The wilderness generation's failure is used to prove that no promise of rest can ever remain.
Joshua's entry is treated as exhausting every possible meaning of rest, leaving the audience no response.
questions.a: The earlier failure serves as a warning while the later appeal to Today shows the promise still addresses hearers.
questions.x: Hebrews combines warning from unbelief with the continuing promise and the later scriptural Today.

questions.q: Which description preserves the distinction between the proposal being debated and the council's resulting letter?
c: The letter rejects circumcision and therefore includes no instructions for Gentile believers at all.
The debate is only about choosing a travel route and never concerns requirements for Gentile believers.
A demand for circumcision and keeping Moses' law is rejected, while specific instructions are still sent to Gentile believers.
The letter adopts the full initial demand for circumcision as the condition of salvation.
questions.a: A demand for circumcision and keeping Moses' law is rejected, while specific instructions are still sent to Gentile believers.
questions.x: The initial proposal and Peter's response concern the larger burden; the final letter gives specified instructions.

questions.q: What evidence does Peter emphasize when explaining his actions concerning Cornelius' household?
c: They first completed circumcision, so Peter could present them as already meeting the critics' demand.
They purchased acceptance with an offering large enough to establish their sincerity.
They promised to conceal their Gentile identity before Peter agreed to act.
The Spirit came on them as on the earlier believers, which challenges his critics' grounds for withholding acceptance.
questions.a: The Spirit came on them as on the earlier believers, which challenges his critics' grounds for withholding acceptance.
questions.x: Peter appeals to the shared gift and recalls Jesus' words; the hearers then acknowledge repentance to life among Gentiles.

questions.q: The fig-tree episode surrounds the temple action in Mark's narrative. Which interpretation stays closest to the described sequence without claiming an explanation the text never states?
c: The arrangement explicitly says every tree in Jerusalem was destroyed because merchants had bought its fruit.
The temple action is narrated before Jesus first encounters the tree, so the two events cannot frame one another.
The disciples are told that forgiveness no longer matters after the tree withers.
The arrangement invites reading the fruitless-tree judgment beside the temple confrontation, while the later dialogue also stresses faith and forgiveness.
questions.a: The arrangement invites reading the fruitless-tree judgment beside the temple confrontation, while the later dialogue also stresses faith and forgiveness.
questions.x: The first tree encounter precedes the temple action; the withered tree follows, and the ensuing instruction includes forgiveness.

questions.q: Which inference is supported by reading the prayer's forgiveness language alongside the unforgiving-servant parable?
c: The different debt sizes prove that only offenses of identical value can be forgiven.
Seeking forgiveness while refusing it to others is treated as a serious contradiction, illustrated by the servant's unequal debts.
The parable teaches that receiving mercy removes every responsibility toward a fellow servant.
The prayer permits refusal to forgive whenever the other person's debt is smaller.
questions.a: Seeking forgiveness while refusing it to others is treated as a serious contradiction, illustrated by the servant's unequal debts.
questions.x: Both passages connect receiving and extending forgiveness; the parable makes the refusal stark through the debt contrast.

questions.q: How does the movement from the women's report to the later gathering resist the claim that the disciples simply expected resurrection and accepted every report immediately?
c: The later gathering concludes that no evidence of resurrection should be considered.
The narrative includes disbelief and confusion before later recognition and Jesus' demonstration at the gathering.
The women are immediately believed without hesitation by everyone who hears them.
No report is brought to the disciples until after Jesus has already eaten in their presence.
questions.a: The narrative includes disbelief and confusion before later recognition and Jesus' demonstration at the gathering.
questions.x: Luke records rejection of the women's words, Peter's wondering, and later fear and difficulty believing before further demonstration.

questions.q: Which description best identifies the reused imagery while respecting the difference between the two settings?
c: The tree in Revelation is identified as the tree of the knowledge of good and evil rather than the tree of life.
River and tree-of-life imagery reappear in a city vision centered on God's throne, rather than simply reproducing the garden scene unchanged.
Revelation replaces all garden imagery with a scene containing neither water nor trees.
Genesis locates its river at the throne of God and the Lamb, exactly as Revelation does.
questions.a: River and tree-of-life imagery reappear in a city vision centered on God's throne, rather than simply reproducing the garden scene unchanged.
questions.x: Revelation reuses life-giving river and tree imagery in its city-and-throne setting.

questions.q: How does Jesus answer concern about greatness across these two scenes?
c: He affirms that the disciples should copy the rulers' way of exercising authority over others.
He resolves the concern by promising every disciple an identical political office immediately.
He treats service as appropriate only before a disciple has achieved genuine greatness.
He contrasts domination with service and uses his own service to reframe greatness among the disciples.
questions.a: He contrasts domination with service and uses his own service to reframe greatness among the disciples.
questions.x: Both scenes contrast prevailing rank assumptions with service, and both relate that contrast to Jesus himself.

questions.q: Which statement accurately distinguishes Jeremiah's promise from Hebrews' use of it?
c: Jeremiah promises a new covenant; Hebrews quotes that promise while presenting Jesus as mediator of a better covenant.
Jeremiah names Jesus of Nazareth directly, so Hebrews needs no argument connecting promise and mediator.
Hebrews quotes the promise in order to deny that Jeremiah ever anticipated a covenant different from the earlier one.
Both texts describe the new covenant only as an increase in the number of written regulations.
questions.a: Jeremiah promises a new covenant; Hebrews quotes that promise while presenting Jesus as mediator of a better covenant.
questions.x: Jeremiah describes covenant renewal with inward law and forgiveness; Hebrews places the quotation in its argument about Jesus' mediation.
